stimulus.text:
0340. Hour 18 of a 24-hour shift. A single-storey house fire, knocked down. Two firefighters went into the basement to check for extension; one is now being carried out unresponsive, and command wants him in your truck immediately.

You are parked on a narrow street. A second engine is manoeuvring past you and a crowd has come out to watch.

En route, securing an intravenous line in a moving ambulance, the patient moves and the used catheter needle catches the back of your hand through the glove.

He is pronounced in the emergency department forty minutes later. Your supervisor meets you in the corridor, tells you a mandatory debriefing is booked for the whole crew at 0900, and asks whether you can pick up the next shift because somebody has called in sick.

items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Workforce Safety and Wellness.

items.stem: An unresponsive firefighter carried out of a basement. What should that raise before you touch him?

options.text: An atmosphere that is still dangerous — carbon monoxide, other products of combustion, or oxygen displacement
options.rationale: The basement did this to a firefighter in protective equipment. It has not stopped.

options.text: That he has had a cardiac event unrelated to the fire
options.rationale: Possible, and not the thing that changes anyone’s safety in the next minute.

options.text: That he was struck by falling material
options.rationale: It would not explain an unresponsive patient with no obvious injury.

options.text: Nothing in particular — treat as an unresponsive adult
options.rationale: The location is the single most informative finding you have.

items.explanation_md: The environment that produced the patient is the first piece of the history, and on this call it is the part that protects you.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Workforce Safety and Wellness.

items.stem: A second engine is manoeuvring past you on a narrow street with a crowd out. What matters most?

options.text: Where you stand while loading — a moving apparatus in a tight street is the immediate physical risk
options.rationale: Being struck by a vehicle is one of the two ways this job kills people.

options.text: Crowd control for the onlookers
options.rationale: It matters and it is not the thing most likely to injure you in the next two minutes.

options.text: Repositioning your ambulance for a faster exit
options.rationale: Useful later; it does not address where your feet are now.

options.text: Nothing — the scene is under fire command
options.rationale: Command does not stand where you are standing.

items.explanation_md: The fire is out and the vehicles are still moving. That is the point in these calls at which people get hurt, because everyone has relaxed.
items.source_ref: NIOSH and NHTSA data on EMS worker fatalities and roadway operations; 23 CFR 634 (high-visibility apparel).

items.stem: The needle catches the back of your hand. What do you do about it, and when?

options.text: Wash it with soap and water as soon as the patient is safe, and report it before the end of this call
options.rationale: Washing first, reporting immediately — the prophylaxis window is measured in hours.

options.text: Squeeze the site to express blood, then continue
options.rationale: No evidence supports squeezing, and it damages tissue.

options.text: Report it at the end of the shift with the rest of the paperwork
options.rationale: That delay can cost the entire benefit of post-exposure prophylaxis.

options.text: Nothing — it went through a glove
options.rationale: A glove reduces inoculum. It does not make this a non-event.

items.explanation_md: The patient is still your responsibility, and this does not wait until the shift ends. Hand over, wash, report, and let the process start.
items.source_ref: CDC/USPHS guidance on occupational post-exposure management of HBV, HCV and HIV.

items.stem: What must your employer provide following this exposure?

options.text: A confidential medical evaluation at no cost to you
options.rationale: Required under the bloodborne pathogens standard.

options.text: Post-exposure follow-up, including serological testing over time
options.rationale: Part of the required follow-up.

options.text: Hepatitis B vaccination at no cost, if you are not already immune
options.rationale: Offered at no cost, and you may have declined it earlier and changed your mind.

options.text: Access to the written exposure control plan
options.rationale: It must exist and be available to you.

options.text: A guarantee of the source patient’s test results
options.rationale: Source testing is sought through the process, and it is not something you are guaranteed.

items.explanation_md: These are obligations under the standard, not favours. Knowing them is what lets you ask for the right thing at 0500 when nobody is keen to start paperwork.
items.source_ref: OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard, 29 CFR 1910.1030.

items.stem: You are asked to pick up the next shift at hour 18 of 24. What is the defensible answer?

options.text: Decline, and say plainly that you are not fit to work it safely
options.rationale: Naming it is the professional act, and it is the one the guideline exists to make possible.

options.text: Accept, and manage it with caffeine
options.rationale: Caffeine helps and does not return an impaired provider to baseline.

options.text: Accept, since refusing leaves the service short
options.rationale: The shortfall is the roster’s problem, and it is not solved by an unfit crew.

options.text: Accept, but ask not to drive
options.rationale: Not driving reduces one risk, and you are still delivering clinical care impaired.

items.explanation_md: Shifts shorter than 24 hours is a guideline recommendation. Being asked to extend one past 30, straight after this call, is exactly the situation it was written about.
items.source_ref: Patterson PD et al., Evidence-Based Guidelines for Fatigue Risk Management in EMS. Prehosp Emerg Care 2018;22(sup1):89–101.

items.stem: A mandatory debriefing is booked for the whole crew at 0900. What is the evidence-based objection?

options.text: Compelling everyone exposed to a single session is not supported, and one trial found worse symptoms a year on
options.rationale: Offer it. Requiring it is the part the evidence does not support.

options.text: Debriefing is harmful in every form and should never be offered
options.rationale: That overstates the finding in the other direction.

options.text: It should be held sooner, within an hour
options.rationale: Timing is not what the objection rests on.

options.text: There is no objection — mandatory sessions are standard practice
options.rationale: Widespread practice is not evidence, which is the point of 1.6.

items.explanation_md: Two things can be true: people need support after this call, and compelling all of them into one session is not the way to give it.
items.source_ref: Rose S et al., Psychological debriefing for preventing PTSD (Cochrane, 2002); NICE NG116 (2018); WHO mhGAP guidance.

items.stem: Over the month after this call, is each response supported?

rows.label: Practical support, rest, and contact with people you trust
A planned check-in, with a route into care if symptoms persist
A compulsory session for everyone on the crew tomorrow morning
Alcohol to get to sleep after the night shifts

items.explanation_md: Everything on the supported side is unremarkable and reachable. That is usually what the evidence turns out to favour.
items.source_ref: Rose S et al., Psychological debriefing for preventing PTSD (Cochrane, 2002); NICE NG116 (2018); WHO mhGAP guidance.
